pr_title: Unify `FixedTime` and `Time` while fixing several problems
pr_body:
# Objective

Current `FixedTime` and `Time` have several problems. This pull aims to fix many of them at once.

- If there is a longer pause between app updates, time will jump forward a lot at once and fixed time will iterate on `FixedUpdate` for a large number of steps. If the pause is merely seconds, then this will just mean jerkiness and possible unexpected behaviour in gameplay. If the pause is hours/days as with OS suspend, the game will appear to freeze until it has caught up with real time.
- If calculating a fixed step takes longer than specified fixed step period, the game will enter a death spiral where rendering each frame takes longer and longer due to more and more fixed step updates being run per frame and the game appears to freeze.
- There is no way to see current fixed step elapsed time inside fixed steps. In order to track this, the game designer needs to add a custom system inside `FixedUpdate` that calculates elapsed or step count in a resource.
- Access to delta time inside fixed step is `FixedStep::period` rather than `Time::delta`. This, coupled with the issue that `Time::elapsed` isn't available at all for fixed steps, makes it that time requiring systems are either implemented to be run in `FixedUpdate` or `Update`, but rarely work in both.
- Fixes #8800 
- Fixes #8543 
- Fixes #7439
- Fixes #5692

## Solution

- Create a generic `Time<T>` clock that has no processing logic but which can be instantiated for multiple usages. This is also exposed for users to add custom clocks.
- Create three standard clocks, `Time<Real>`, `Time<Virtual>` and `Time<Fixed>`, all of which contain their individual logic.
- Create one "default" clock, which is just `Time` (or `Time<()>`), which will be overwritten from `Time<Virtual>` on each update, and `Time<Fixed>` inside `FixedUpdate` schedule. This way systems that do not care specifically which time they track can work both in `Update` and `FixedUpdate` without changes and the behaviour is intuitive.
- Add `max_delta` to virtual time update, which limits how much can be added to virtual time by a single update. This fixes both the behaviour after a long freeze, and also the death spiral by limiting how many fixed timestep iterations there can be per update. Possible future work could be adding `max_accumulator` to add a sort of "leaky bucket" time processing to possibly smooth out jumps in time while keeping frame rate stable.
- Many minor tweaks and clarifications to the time functions and their documentation.

## Changelog

- `Time::raw_delta()`, `Time::raw_elapsed()` and related methods are moved to `Time<Real>::delta()` and `Time<Real>::elapsed()` and now match `Time` API
- `FixedTime` is now `Time<Fixed>` and matches `Time` API. 
- `Time<Fixed>` default timestep is now 64 Hz, or 15625 microseconds.
- `Time` inside `FixedUpdate` now reflects fixed timestep time, making systems portable between `Update ` and `FixedUpdate`.
- `Time::pause()`, `Time::set_relative_speed()` and related methods must now be called as `Time<Virtual>::pause()` etc.
- There is a new `max_delta` setting in `Time<Virtual>` that limits how much the clock can jump by a single update. The default value is 0.25 seconds.
- Removed `on_fixed_timer()` condition as `on_timer()` does the right thing inside `FixedUpdate` now.

## Migration Guide

- Change all `Res<Time>` instances that access `raw_delta()`, `raw_elapsed()` and related methods to `Res<Time<Real>>` and `delta()`, `elapsed()`, etc.
- Change access to `period` from `Res<FixedTime>` to `Res<Time<Fixed>>` and use `delta()`.
- The default timestep has been changed from 60 Hz to 64 Hz. If you wish to restore the old behaviour, use `app.insert_resource(Time::<Fixed>::from_hz(60.0))`.
- Change `app.insert_resource(FixedTime::new(duration))` to `app.insert_resource(Time::<Fixed>::from_duration(duration))`
- Change `app.insert_resource(FixedTime::new_from_secs(secs))` to `app.insert_resource(Time::<Fixed>::from_seconds(secs))`
- Change `system.on_fixed_timer(duration)` to `system.on_timer(duration)`. Timers in systems placed in `FixedUpdate` schedule automatically use the fixed time clock.
- Change `ResMut<Time>` calls to `pause()`, `is_paused()`, `set_relative_speed()`  and related methods to `ResMut<Time<Virtual>>` calls. The API is the same, with the exception that `relative_speed()` will return the actual last ste relative speed, while `effective_relative_speed()` returns 0.0 if the time is paused and corresponds to the speed that was set when the update for the current frame started.

## Todo

- [x] Update pull name and description
- [x] Top level documentation on usage
- [x] Fix examples
- [x] Decide on default `max_delta` value
- [x] Decide naming of the three clocks: is `Real`, `Virtual`, `Fixed` good?
- [x] Decide if the three clock inner structures should be in prelude
- [x] Decide on best way to configure values at startup: is manually inserting a new clock instance okay, or should there be config struct separately?
- [x] Fix links in docs
- [x] Decide what should be public and what not
- [x] Decide how `wrap_period` should be handled when it is changed
- [x] ~~Add toggles to disable setting the clock as default?~~ No, separate pull if needed.
- [x] Add tests
- [x] Reformat, ensure adheres to conventions etc.
- [x] Build documentation and see that it looks correct

## Contributors

Huge thanks to @alice-i-cecile and @maniwani while building this pull. It was a shared effort!

Still reviewing. Most things look good! However:

> `Time::set_wrap_period` no longer accepts wrap periods with a subsecond component. It is very unlikely anybody uses those.

I've commented on #8912, but this change does not belong here. I disagree that the "complexity" of the mod/rem calculation is an issue. Imposing a user-facing limit to "fix" an internal implementation detail is an issue though.

I prefer not to have variants like `Time::delta_seconds` that only do type conversions, as they might make unnecessary type conversions. 🛡️

```rust
let x = Duration::from_secs_f32(time.delta_seconds()); // I know they wouldn't do this
``` 

What do you all think about this?

> I prefer not to have variants like `Time::delta_seconds` that only do type conversions, as they might make unnecessary type conversions.

I think the point has been caching. Converting a `Duration` into  an `f32`/`f64` isn't free. There's a few arithmetic instructions involved. The cost is negligible, but last I checked (w/ godbolt) the compiler sometimes doesn't figure out it can elide multiple `time.delta_seconds()` calls if you don't cache the value.

IMO there's no reason to do unnecessary work every time `time.delta_seconds()` is called, or make you assign it to a local variable, when we can just cache it internally.

> (I have a feeling that major changes will still be needed after the merge. What shall we do?)

My personal view: 0.11 has just been released. If this gets merged fast, then we maximize the amount of people that gets subjected to these changes before release - so maximize the amount of feedback we get before 0.12. I will be around to make further pulls during this release cycle, so I can also react to feedback.

I personally think it's super annoying to have the API blow up just because we want multiple different types of the same value, and just for caching reasons. I considered making PrecomputedDuration as well, which would share 100% of the Duration API, but just would ensure that Duration.as_secs_f32() would be precomputed and saved (or lazily computed if that ends up being a performance win).

However, I didn't want to touch that discussion with this pull. I'm simply preserving what was the behaviour in the previous version, and I'd suggest a new pull is made to clean up all the usages of `duration_seconds` etc. if we decide to get rid of them.

> I personally think it's super annoying to have the API blow up just because we want multiple different types of the same value, and just for caching reasons.

> I considered making a `PrecomputedDuration` as well, which would share 100% of the `Duration` API but would keep `Duration.as_secs_f32()` [cached] (or lazily computed if that ends up being a performance win).

I do see where you're coming from.

True, we could use our own variant of `Duration` with internal caching to remove the cost of `time.delta().as_secs_f32()`, but yeah I think you should try that in a separate PR. That doesn't have to be a follow-up though, it could be merged before this one is.

(I'd suggest something like `CachedDuration` or `CachedFloatDuration` as the name though.)

Still, I'm not sure if we should remove the `time.delta_seconds()` method in favor of `time.delta().as_secs_f32()`. The `f32` value is the most commonly used, and such a change would make getting it less ergonomic. So yeah, IMO do a separate PR with that change and then ask cart to review it.

In the design phase I got some opposition to doing this with `Deref`, as it was felt to be too implicit. Also, even though Bevy differs in many places already, from Rust docs:

> Implementing Deref for smart pointers makes accessing the data behind them convenient, which is why they implement Deref. On the other hand, the rules regarding Deref and [DerefMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.DerefMut.html) were designed specifically to accommodate smart pointers. Because of this, **Deref should only be implemented for smart pointers to avoid confusion.**

Honestly could've gone either way. `Deref` is more "traditional", where as wrapping the specialization makes it more explicit. If this final design would be converted to `Deref`, I'm not sure the initial opposition to `Deref` would still hold.

issue_context.title: `FixedUpdate` schedules that take too long enter a cascading failure mode
issue_context.body:
## Bevy version

0.10

## What you did

Run a fixed time schedule that takes longer to complete than the allocated time.

## What went wrong

As the schedule took longer than the `FixedTime::period`, the accumulated time increases.

The next time we need to run the fixed update schedule, we must run it *more* times in order to catch up.

This puts us even further behind, worsening the problem...

I talked in Discord how time could be tracked per system – so `time.delta()` in that system would calculate the delta since the last time that system was run. However, that was deemed too complex. 

Explicitly tracking time deltas requires the user to store the previous `time.elapsed()` value somewhere. `Instant::duration_since` equivalent is simply `time.elapsed() - since`. `Time::elapsed` is the `Instant` equivalent inside Bevy, one that isn't platform specific mess like Instant, and `duration_since` is just substraction. Also `checked_sub` and `saturating_sub` are available for Durations if there's a need for specific underflow behaviour.

> I talked in Discord how time could be tracked per system – so `time.delta()` in that system would calculate the delta since the last time that system was run. However, that was deemed too complex.

For a few reasons.

1. We can't actually auto-update `Time` with this per-system value. `Time` can't even be used inside `bevy_ecs` because `bevy_time` depends on `bevy_ecs`.
2. Using a unique `Δt` per system is not even a valid way to intergrate time. The same sequence of logic would get different results depending on how many systems it was split into. It's super suspect that different components on the same entity could be integrated by different amounts of time.
3. It's too different from what everyone knows "delta time" normally means. It'd also break unity with fixed update, which is counterproductive.
Maybe that's right. This was probably not good idea.
Why would you want to manually set a timestep in bullet time when you can use `set_relative_speed(0.1)` for example?
At `0.1` the fixed update would run at one tenth the rate it usually does which likely not going to be enough for e.g. physics to look right

> not enough for physics to look right

IIRC it's about responsiveness. `set_relative_speed(0.1)` slows things down 10x. So 60 ticks/sec would drop to 6 ticks/sec. If you want player movement to be responsive within bullet time, 6 times a second isn't much.

If you change the timestep itself, then yeah, the math is different, but you can maintain the same tick rate.

If there's something that can be added to the doc string to make the intention even clearer, please let me know!

The only cases where timestep might have to be modified when the game is running is if the relative speed of the game gets slowed down so much that the orginal timestamp results in jerky physics (objects reacting to collisions at 6 FPS for example) or if the relative speed is sped up so much (like 8192x acceleration in submarine games) that simulating with the original timestep would be prohibitively expensive to do.

Generics are used only for code decoration. In such cases, codes are simpler without generics.

If you want to make some common code, you can provide default implementations in the trait.

The aim is to provide a standard Time/Clock structure that can be used for multiple separate clocks and used in an equivalent manner. There's five choices in how to make this happen:

1. Wrap a common clock structure, but privately. External API uses same method names (like `delta` and `elapsed`) but has no relation typewise. I dislike this solution a lot – if that gets picked, somebody else has to write the pull.
2. Wrap a common clock structure, and expose something like `pub fn clock(&self) -> &Clock` to retrieve it. That means that every user of `Time` needs to change their code from `time.elapsed()` to `time.clock().elapsed()`.
3. Wrap a common clock structure, and provide automatic `Deref` to `Clock`, so that `time.elapsed()` may still work, but it's unintuitive because of the deref magic.
4. Invert the relationship and make `Time` wrap the clock specific data, and specialize the specific methods on that structure. That's what's done in this pull.
5. Create a new `Clock` trait which has `elapsed()`, `delta()` etc. and implement it for multiple structs. Internal implentation sharing has to be done somehow as well.

Out of these five choices, what I picked is what I think is the best approach. If there's a well founded argument, and consensus, that some other choice out of these five should be picked, I'm happy to adapt the code if I agree with the approach.

FWIW, I think the current approach in this pull is "neat", but I'd rather have a simpler solution without generics. But right now I think it's the least bad choice.

Also `checked_sub` and `saturating_sub` are available for Durations if there's a need for specific underflow behaviour.

> I talked in Discord how time could be tracked per system – so `time.delta()` in that system would calculate the delta since the last time that system was run. However, that was deemed too complex.

For a few reasons.

1. We can't actually auto-update `Time` with this per-system value. `Time` can't even be used inside `bevy_ecs` because `bevy_time` depends on `bevy_ecs`.
2. Using a unique `Δt` per system is not even a valid way to intergrate time. The same sequence of logic would get different results depending on how many systems it was split into. It's super suspect that different components on the same entity could be integrated by different amounts of time.
3. It's too different from what everyone knows "delta time" normally means. It'd also break unity with fixed update, which is counterproductive.

Generics are used only for code decoration. In such cases, codes are simpler without generics.

If you want to make some common code, you can provide default implementations in the trait.

The aim is to provide a standard Time/Clock structure that can be used for multiple separate clocks and used in an equivalent manner. There's five choices in how to make this happen:

1. Wrap a common clock structure, but privately. External API uses same method names (like `delta` and `elapsed`) but has no relation typewise. I dislike this solution a lot – if that gets picked, somebody else has to write the pull.
2. Wrap a common clock structure, and expose something like `pub fn clock(&self) -> &Clock` to retrieve it. That means that every user of `Time` needs to change their code from `time.elapsed()` to `time.clock().elapsed()`.
3. Wrap a common clock structure, and provide automatic `Deref` to `Clock`, so that `time.elapsed()` may still work, but it's unintuitive because of the deref magic.
4. Invert the relationship and make `Time` wrap the clock specific data, and specialize the specific methods on that structure. That's what's done in this pull.
5. Create a new `Clock` trait which has `elapsed()`, `delta()` etc. and implement it for multiple structs. Internal implentation sharing has to be done somehow as well.

Out of these five choices, what I picked is what I think is the best approach. If there's a well founded argument, and consensus, that some other choice out of these five should be picked, I'm happy to adapt the code if I agree with the approach.

FWIW, I think the current approach in this pull is "neat", but I'd rather have a simpler solution without generics. But right now I think it's the least bad choice.

Why would you want to manually set a timestep in bullet time when you can use `set_relative_speed(0.1)` for example?
At `0.1` the fixed update would run at one tenth the rate it usually does which likely not going to be enough for e.g. physics to look right

> not enough for physics to look right

IIRC it's about responsiveness. `set_relative_speed(0.1)` slows things down 10x. So 60 ticks/sec would drop to 6 ticks/sec. If you want player movement to be responsive within bullet time, 6 times a second isn't much.

If you change the timestep itself, then yeah, the math is different, but you can maintain the same tick rate.

If there's something that can be added to the doc string to make the intention even clearer, please let me know!

The only cases where timestep might have to be modified when the game is running is if the relative speed of the game gets slowed down so much that the orginal timestamp results in jerky physics (objects reacting to collisions at 6 FPS for example) or if the relative speed is sped up so much (like 8192x acceleration in submarine games) that simulating with the original timestep would be prohibitively expensive to do.
Since this cache is recalculated whenever time advances, no performance improvement can be expected. It is okay to retain only the ~~pre-calculated~~ value before calculation.

Comments in pull discussion on this as well. I'd be happy to remove precalculated cache, and even happer would be to get rid of the overly duplicated API, but I didn't want to make that decision in this pull, since it's also controversial.

The difference is so very small that it cannot be measured in the benchmark, so no one will notice if you change this silently. 🏃 

The current code computes `6 * 3` times per frame, which may be slower than not caching.

There's four choices:
1. Leave as is, figure out something in another pull if it feels meaningful.
2. Remove precomputation, but keep the same API, so `delta_seconds()` will return `f32`, just calculated on every request.
3. Create `CachedDuration` which keeps precomputation, and change API to return only `CachedDuration`, forcing every user to change `time.delta_seconds()` to `time.delta().as_secs_f32()` but keeping same performance "advantage".
4. Remove precomputation and change API to return only `Duration`. Every user needs to switch from `time.delta_seconds()` to `time.delta().as_secs_f32()`, but it will be the Rust standard `Duration` class so it should be quite obvious. (Not sure what to do about wrapped time here...)

In a way, I do understand the precomputation – even if there's `6 * 3` computation per frame to get the values, most of which will not be used, it's still a meaningless amount of time. Where as if there is one `time.delta_seconds()` call in a system which does collision detection, for example, then that's easily millions of conversions to float per frame... if the compiler for some reason doesn't optimize it outside the loops.

But I think what you are proposing is number two? I'm fine with switching this pull to do that, if I can count on not having to revert my changes in a few days :-)
